reception.text: To the coal operators and conservative opinion, a president who called capital and labor to the White House as equals and stood ready to send the Army into private mines had claimed a power the Constitution did not give him.
Attorney General Philander Knox and much of the legal profession thought the plan to seize the mines indefensible.
To organized labor the intervention was a deliverance: the first time the federal government was used to bring an employer to the table rather than to break a strike.
John Mitchell called the new Board of Conciliation a victory, even though the union won no recognition.

political_impact.text: A White House statement issued at 2:20 a.m. named the Anthracite Coal Strike Commission, filling the operators' "sociologist" category with E. E. Clark of the Order of Railway Conductors; Roosevelt added Bishop John L. Spalding on his own authority.
political_impact.source: Evening Star and Indianapolis Journal, October 16, 1902; Commission Report, p. 14

political_impact.text: The Wilkes-Barre miners' convention voted to end the strike on October 21, and the men went back to work on October 23.

The commission's award gave contract miners a ten percent raise, shorter days to some classes of company men, a sliding wage scale and a Board of Conciliation, running to March 31, 1906, but no union recognition.
political_impact.source: Report to the President on the Anthracite Coal Strike (S. Doc. 6, 58th Cong., Spec. Sess., 1903)

political_impact.text: Congress created the Department of Commerce and Labor while the commission was still hearing the case; the strike added momentum to the push for a cabinet voice for labor, which Roosevelt had proposed in 1901.

legacy.text: The strike is generally marked as the first time the federal government stepped into a major labor dispute as an umpire for the public rather than as a strikebreaker.
A separate cabinet Department of Labor was created in 1913; its first secretary, William B. Wilson, had been secretary of the 1902 Wilkes-Barre convention that ended the strike.
Roosevelt later described the duty of the President as "the steward of the people," telling the strike story right after it; scholars call this the stewardship theory.
legacy.source: Theodore Roosevelt, An Autobiography (1913), ch. XIII

legacy.text: The settlement left union recognition unresolved, and those questions were fought over for another generation.
